title: Adversarial training significantly reduces adaptive white-box PGD success

invariants.description: PGD L∞ ε=0.3 must still evade the undefended model (observed 39.3–40.7% in 7 numerical environments).

On the same test samples, the adaptive attack must succeed significantly less often against the adversarially trained model than against the undefended one (exact one-sided McNemar test, α = 0.05 fixed in advance; observed p ≤ 0.0038 in 7 environments).
Adversarial training must remove at least 5 percentage points of adaptive attack success (≈ 7 of 145 samples; observed 8.3–14.6 pp).
Adversarial training must remove at least 15% of the undefended adaptive success (observed 20.7–36.8%).

Residual adaptive success for THIS pinned configuration (seed 7) must stay ≤ 35% (observed 25.0–31.7% across 7 environments). Not a property of adversarial training in general: across seeds 0–9 the residual ranges 25.5–43.4%. This is a reduction, not immunity.

rationale: Adaptive evaluation: the attacker has white-box access to the adversarially trained model. The defense claim is comparative, so the primary invariants compare undefended and defended success on the SAME samples. The former single bound (≤ 30%) was calibrated in one numerical environment and failed in 3 of 7 with no code change, because the BLAS kernel changes MLP training and the adaptive attack amplifies it; see docs/regression-analysis-mlb-reg-002.md.
